units: a living culture forms from flour and water left open to the air
yeasts present in the atmosphere settle into the mixture
the baker removes a portion and tops it up with fresh flour at regular intervals
after a week the culture becomes steady
a sour smell signals that the culture can be used
the flour is sifted before the warm liquid goes in
the dough is folded over on itself between two rest periods
the fierce heat of the oven sets the structure and colors the outside
the resulting bread keeps for a week without drying out
text: A starter begins with nothing more than flour, water, and the open air of the room. Give it two or three nights and wild yeasts drift in out of that air, settle into the paste, and puff it up. From then on the baker feeds the culture on a schedule: scoop out part of what sits in the jar, stir in a measure of fresh flour, and wait. By the end of the first week the culture holds steady and gives off a sharp, sour smell, and that smell is the signal that it can raise a full dough. Sift the flour, pour in warm water, work the starter through with a spatula, and knead until the mass turns soft and supple. Let it rest, fold it over on itself, let it rest again. A blistering oven sets the crumb and browns the outside. The method asks for patience. What it returns is a dense, fragrant loaf that keeps a week without drying out.

units: a worker at an inn leaves her pot on weak embers before going to bed
she had meant to take it off before sunrise
tiredness keeps her from coming back at the planned hour
the liquid drops by half and the meat falls apart into strands
the cook skims the surface and then tastes the dish
the sauce turns out thick and slightly sweet
the low prolonged heat has changed the tissue of the meat
the customers ask for the same dish the next day
the cook repeats the accident on purpose every evening
text: A cook at a roadside inn set her heavy pot over dying embers and went up to bed, certain she would lift it off before sunrise. She slept through instead. When she came back down, the broth had boiled away by half and the meat had fallen apart into strands. She skimmed the surface, expecting to find ruin, and tasted from the edge of the ladle. What she found was thick, dark, and faintly sweet. Because the heat had stayed so low for so long, the tough tissue had melted instead of tightening. The travelers sitting at her tables asked for the same dish the following day. She could not explain the accident, so she chose to repeat it on purpose: every evening she banked the fire down and left the pot alone until morning. A recipe born of forgetfulness made the name of the house.

units: lumps form in a sauce while it cooks
the pan has to come off the heat source at once
leaving the sauce on the heat gives a scorched taste
adding a cold liquid and then whisking hard dissolves most of the lumps
the shift in temperature makes the lumps give way
a fine strainer catches the pieces that remain
the leftover bits are crushed with the back of a hollow utensil
the mixture then goes back over a low flame with constant stirring
stirring the flour into cold liquid prevents the trouble next time
text: Lumps showing up in your sauce while it cooks? Nothing is lost yet. Pull the pan off the burner right away, because leaving it there lets the flour stick to the bottom and pick up a scorched taste. Splash in a little cold water and whisk hard, right there in the pan. That jolt in temperature breaks most of the lumps apart. If a few stubborn ones hang on, tip the whole thing through a fine strainer and press the stubborn bits against the mesh with the back of a ladle. Then set it over a low flame again and keep stirring without a pause, circling out to the sides of the pan so nothing catches. Next time, stir your flour into a cold liquid before it ever meets the heat, and none of this happens. A smooth sauce comes down to that one habit, not to some knack nobody taught you. Keep the whisk where you can grab it.

units: two cooking counters face each other in a covered hall
the first counter cooks everything by plunging it into hot fat
the line at the first counter moves quickly
the second counter has been simmering its dishes since early morning
customers in a hurry choose the fast cooking
the prices at the two counters are close
their spending goes to different things
the woman in charge of the place notices that the traffic flips over the course of the week
neither counter tries to copy the other
text: Inside a covered market hall, two cooking counters face each other across the aisle and argue, without saying a word, about method. On one side everything goes down into hot fat: the heat seals the outside in a matter of seconds, and the line never stops moving. On the other, a cook has had pots simmering since the morning opened, and her service runs at a slower pace. Customers in a hurry pick the fryer, and those who sit down to eat pick the pot. The prices on the two boards land close together, though the two spend on different things, one burning through oil, the other through hours of fuel. The woman who runs the hall notices the traffic flip as the week goes on, quick early, patient by the end. Neither counter shows any interest in copying its neighbor, and the quiet rivalry keeps the hall full.

units: the goods on the stall are sorted by shade
the first group gathers dried roots and barks
the red goods give off a smell that catches at the throat
the green goods sit at the back of the stall
a stone vessel takes up the middle of the stall
the inside of the vessel is stained by past mixtures
a worn grating tool is kept for hard dried fruits
the seller refuses to sell goods already reduced to powder
he claims that powder loses its fragrance within one season
text: At the spice seller's stall the goods are laid out and sorted by shade. The ochres come first: dried roots, curls of bark, powders that smell of resin and warm wood. The reds sit next to them, harsher, sharp enough to catch at the back of your throat when you reach across the table. The greens fill the back, crumpled leaves, seeds no bigger than grit, stems tied into tight bundles. A stone mortar holds the middle of the table, its pestle leaning, its inner wall stained by mixtures long since sold. Beside it lies a worn grater kept for the hard dried nuts, which the seller will not hand over already ground. Powder goes flat within a single season, he says, while the whole seed keeps its soul. Behind him, cloth sacks slump open on brown treasures nobody knows the names of, and nobody ever asks for.

units: cooking once rested on the senses of the cook
measuring probes changed the nature of the trade
each food can now be given a set band of heat
baths of regulated heat appeared afterward
food sealed away from the air never goes past the target value
the writer judges this change a good one
opponents read it as a loss of feel
the writer holds that the instrument rules out crude error without dictating taste
what the writer fears most is the sameness of the results
text: For generations cooking ran on the senses alone: a palm held over the coals, an ear tuned to the sizzle, an eye on the color of the crust. Then the measuring probe arrived, and the trade turned into something else altogether. A cook could now assign each piece of food a narrow band of heat and hold to it without drifting. The same logic went further with baths of regulated heat, where food sealed away from the air never climbs past its target. I take that shift for progress, whatever is said by those who read it as a loss of feel. Measuring does not forbid tasting. The instrument rules out the crude failure; it has nothing to say about seasoning. What worries me sits elsewhere, in the pull toward sameness. A flawless result repeated without variation turns into a flawless kind of boredom.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the pastry cook comes from a line of millers
her father sorted grain in front of her during her childhood
she could tell one grind from another by touch before she could read a recipe
this early familiarity shaped her choice of trade
she started as an apprentice in a neighborhood workshop
the night hours built up her stamina
a wrist injury pulled her away from kneading
that setback led her toward light preparations
she puts her flour through the sieve twice to get her layered pastry
she refuses to expand her house after a mention in a trade journal
text: The pastry cook at a guest house comes from a long line of millers, and flour has never once been an abstraction to her. Her father sorted grain in front of her when she was small, so she could tell one grind from another by touch before she could read a recipe. That early ease settled her choice of trade. She started out as an apprentice in a neighborhood bakehouse, where the night hours built up her stamina. A wrist injury pulled her away from the kneading bench, and the setback pushed her toward the lighter work of fine doughs. There she found her signature: pale layered pastry whose lift comes from flour put through the sieve twice. Her own apprentices remember one rule above the rest, weigh the gesture instead of rushing it. Since a trade journal named her house, she has refused to grow.

units: the room pleases the visitor right away
the menu offers a narrow choice
the vegetables come out lukewarm although their dish was meant to keep them hot
the reviewer works out that the plates waited under a heat source
the cooking of the main course is correct
the sauce has broken because it was mounted too early
the fault lies with the layout and not with the skills
moving the pass closer to the stove would remove the wait
sending out fewer plates at a time would improve the service
the dessert made to order arrives flawless
text: The room wins you over at once, and the menu is short, which usually promises a kitchen that knows its own mind. Trouble arrives with the first course. The vegetables come out lukewarm in a cast-iron dish that should have kept them scalding hot, and you can tell the plates waited a while under a lamp. The main course confirms the weakness: the cooking is judged well, but the sauce was mounted too early and has already broken on the plate. The fault is not talent, it is layout. Move the pass closer to the stove, send out fewer plates at a time, and the wait that spoils the kitchen's own work would disappear. Dessert proves the point. Made to order, it lands clean, tight, exact. A house capable of that should not let the start of a meal go cold. We will come back, after calling ahead.

units: the reader had asked whether the writer eats better since moving
the writer finds the food different without finding it better
her aunt cooked everything in a single pot
she used the leftovers of the day before in a broth
the roommate gives every ingredient its own utensil
at the aunt's place the helpings were generous and hot
proportions were never argued about there
in the current place people taste and adjust before serving
the writer misses the smell that used to fill the hallway
the writer invites the reader to come and judge for himself
text: You asked me whether I eat any better since the move. Honestly, it is different, not better. My aunt cooked everything out of one pot, and whatever was left from the day before went into a broth and came back as dinner. My roommate works the opposite way around: every ingredient gets its own pan, its own timer, its own seasoning. At her place the food came hot and there was plenty of it, and nobody ever argued about proportions or put a thing on a scale. Here we taste, we adjust, we start over, and supper lands late. I like both, for reasons that cancel each other out. One fed me, the other entertains me. What I miss is the smell that filled the hallway the second I opened her door. This place smells clean. Come over some evening and judge for yourself. We will pick the menu together at the cupboard.

units: the woman in charge of a preserving workshop answers questions about common mistakes
she holds that the quality of the seal counts for more than the thickness of the glass
a seal used a second time often fails as things cool
the liquid has to cover the jars completely during the heat treatment
the top of the contents spoils with no visible sign if it stands clear
she recalls that salt preserves but hides the flaws of poor produce
the foam that appears on fermenting vegetables is no sign of failure
that foam comes with the start of the process
she refuses to state a general rule about how long things keep
text: We put the most common mistakes to the woman who runs a preserving workshop. On the jars themselves, she says the seal matters more than the thickness of the glass, and that a seal used a second time tends to fail as the jar cools. On heat processing she is firm: the water has to cover the jars completely, or the top of the contents spoils with nothing visible to show for it. On salt she draws a line, since it preserves but also hides the flaws of poor produce. Her answer on fermented vegetables surprises us. The foam that rises is no sign of failure, it comes with the start of the process. On how long a jar keeps, she will give no general rule at all, and sends us back to the smell, to the sound of the lid, to the look of the liquid. An attentive keeper's nose, she says, beats any label.
